label: JSON parse + assertions
html:
JSON demo

output is in the console pane.
wren:
import "@hatch:json"   for JSON
import "@hatch:assert" for Expect

var text =
  "{\"package\": \"wlift\"," +
  " \"version\": \"0.4.0\"," +
  " \"targets\": [\"x86_64\", \"aarch64\", \"wasm32\"]," +
  " \"jit\": true}"

var obj = JSON.parse(text)

System.print("name     = %(obj["package"])")
System.print("version  = %(obj["version"])")
System.print("targets  = %(obj["targets"].join(", "))")
System.print("jit      = %(obj["jit"])")

Expect.that(obj["package"]).toBe("wlift")
Expect.that(obj["targets"].count).toBe(3)
Expect.that(obj["jit"]).toBe(true)

// Round-trip through encode/decode.
var encoded = JSON.encode({"hello": "world", "n": 42})
var back = JSON.parse(encoded)
Expect.that(back["n"]).toBe(42)
System.print("✓ round-trip: %(encoded)")

label: SIMD — Simd4f / Simd4i lane ops
html:
SIMD demo

Lane-wise arithmetic, comparisons, bitmask, Float32Array round-trip, and a tier-up throughput pass — output in the console.

Modern browsers run this through wasm simd128 instructions; older ones get the same results via the scalar fallback. Pass 2 of the throughput section measures steady-state JIT speed once the closure has tiered up.

label: Perf — fib(20) tier-up bench
html:
Perf — fib(20) tier-up bench

Recursive compute benchmark — output is in the console pane below.

After ~50 invocations fib's body promotes to a per-function wasm module: recursive calls dispatch through inline call_indirect and the module-var read of fib lands as a 3-instruction i32.load + i64.load triple — no wasm-bindgen boundary per access.

label: Perf — closure upvalue capture bench
html:
Perf — closure upvalue bench

Two flavors of closure-captured state called in tight loops — output in the console pane below.

Both passes tier-up. GetUpvalue lowers to an inline 5-load chain through the cdylib's current_closure cell + the upvalue array; SetUpvalue mirrors the read path, then calls wren_write_barrier for the GC inter-generational hand-off (the only boundary crossing left on the write side). The mutating-capture pass runs ~10× fewer iterations because per-call cost includes that barrier call; the read-only pass shows the bare inline-chain cost.
